utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Joanna Korner, and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, having had the opportunity to think about it, could you alert us as to how much longer you expect you would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I considered this very carefully last night, and I determined that I will need approximately six hours to complete and this is the reason. First, I have to take additional time for these new topics that are raised during this witness examination-in-chief. Despite my learned friend's expression of surprise, though he didn't spent a lot of time on them, to cross-examine on them will require documents and -- and other evidence to be presented to this witness. Secondly, we still need to deal with what we had expected this witness to testify about based upon his 65 ter summary, based upon his prior interviews with the Office of the Prosecution which is the issue of access of the Milos group members to the accused, and the accused access to their intelligence reports. That will require showing this witness a number of documents. And I just note that we have at this stage over 80 Radulovic or Milos group reports in evidence, and this is an issue that -- that has been contested in this case, whether these reports had made it to the RS MUP leadership, and so it's important that we address them with this witness as the Prosecution intended to do during its case in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, taking matters one step at a time, do I infer from what you have said that, notwithstanding what you indicated yesterday, that we should keep the reserved extra session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I would think that -- well, it's hard for me to say how things go. If things go as I would hope they would, we would need today and Thursday to complete my case in-chief and then that would leave Friday for any -- I mean -- I'm sorry, for cross-examination, and Friday, for any re-examination. So I don't think we'd run into any time problems. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. It was the -- you would recall that in terms of the arrangements that been put in place, it included the extra sitting this afternoon. And unless I misunderstood what had you said yesterday, you had on more than one occasion yesterday, as I understood it, indicated that the extra session today would not be necessary. I'm only asking, as I said, without even thinking about what's going to happen after today, taking it one day at a time, whether we should keep the extra session for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't think it's necessary. Because I think six hours should be -- today, regular sittings, and Thursday, regular sittings, that should cover the six hours. Just based upon how we've proceeded so far with evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you seem to be entering a dissent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's only Tuesday today. We have four hours of work and tomorrow another four, that's eight. So my learned friend will finish on Wednesday, not Thursday. That's why I reacted. And if I have any re-direct, and any questions from the Judges, we have full days on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well -- he didn't mention Wednesday because you may recall that yesterday he indicated that with the - there's no other way of putting it - jumping about that would have been necessary tomorrow, it would be simpler to just vacate Wednesday and pick up on Thursday, and I think that's still central on his estimate. So the position is, we don't need the extra session today, we rise at 1.45, and resume ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the more practical and efficient approach would be to retain today's extended session, and we will assess whether we need to pick up any time tomorrow, and go from there. And, of course, Thursday is an afternoon session. But we will sit the extended session that is reserved for today. So unless there are any other housekeeping -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only reason I'm here is because yesterday I made a request that we now be given proper information about what witnesses are going to say 72 hours in advance of their testifying. As you'll recall, the proofing note, five day's worth, was sent to us at 9.00 on Friday, and I rather casually said that Mr. Olmsted, of course, did have the weekend, but what about administrative staff? I should add I'd forgotten that Mr. Olmsted was running in the Amsterdam marathon, and so he had rather less time and I imagine was rather tired on Sunday. But, Your Honours, I do say that this cannot go on like this. The 65 ter summaries are utterly vague, totally useless as far as actually knowing what the witness is going to say, and so I do ask that we now have an order that the proofing notes be delivered 72 hours in advance, particularly as there is now a two-week break when all witnesses can be seen and proofed. The second matter, Your Honours, was whether there is a change in the order of the witnesses. We really would like to know that, because I understand there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, you're still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm just waiting [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before we respond to Ms. Korner's request, do you have a view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Speaking about a possible change of schedule, I said when I talked to Ms. Korner that there is a possibility there would be a change in schedule, but I also told her that at least ten days in advance I would give her notice. Because there's a possibility that a witness who is scheduled to testify first in November would be inversed with the third witness. That means that SZ-007 would be switched with SZ-002. But I just told Ms. Korner that this possibility exists and they would be given sufficient notice and able to prepare. However, this is still not final. I will know next Wednesday, and I will inform both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that -- Mr. Krgovic, so Wednesday week? Because that's not ten days before the witness is due to testify. Not ten working days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wednesday week, because the witness starts on the 8th, on Tuesday, the Prosecution will have notice by the 27th at least at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are asking for at least 10 working days, so that's Monday at the latest. I don't understand the difficulty either, why would he only know next Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honour, I will be in Banja Luka only on Wednesday and will be able only then to look at the documentation and talk to the witness. Because I must say we have certain difficulties with him related to health. So I still have no confirmation of this, and I will have it only on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What was the second point. The first point, do you have a difficulty with the Chamber imposing 72-hour rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. And the reason is that we asked the same standard to be applied as in the Prosecution case. Namely, that as soon as the proofing of a witness is completed here in The Hague, we were supposed to get proofing notes. And it happened in at least ten cases so far that we received the proofing notes the night before the witness's appearance, although the witnesses changed their statements considerably and started mentioning events that had not been mentioned either in prior evidence or in summaries and related directly to the contact of the accused. I will give you just a few references, pages of transcript, 18303 onwards; 16973, onwards; 17413 and onward; 17535 and on. When the Prosecution brought witnesses who spoke about adjudicated facts, let's say, and then led them to testify about the conduct of the accused, and those witnesses started remembering where they had seen Zupljanin and spoke about the accused. And then, on that occasion, the Trial Chamber found that the Defence was not prejudiced in any way and allowed the Prosecution to lead this evidence. This is a drastic example of how the Prosecution behaved and led their evidence. Second, it is baseless for the Prosecution to claim that they don't know what the witnesses would be testifying about. Perhaps the Trial Chamber is not aware of this because you don't have that information. Most of our witnesses had given statements to the Prosecution. They have testified in prior cases, and the Prosecution has that information. I'm speaking about our witnesses, Defence witnesses. Specifically, Mr. Hannis objected that he only has a 65 ter summary and very small proofing notes concerning Witness Jakovic. And he had the transcript of a -- of that witness who testified for a whole day. So there are both interviews with the Prosecution and prior evidence in prior cases. I will speak again about transcript page 11361, when Mr. Pantelic objected in the same way she is objecting now, and she answered exactly as I am now. Namely, that there are interviews. If I may add, all these witnesses - I'm not sure how many but out of the viva voce witnesses perhaps only one or two do not have written statements in the possession of the Prosecution - but all of them speak to the events concerning which the Prosecution has led evidence and introduced documents where these witnesses are mentioned as participants in the events, and that's the reason why we are calling them; namely, that Prosecution witnesses have mentioned them, spoke about their participation in certain events, and they speak to those events. So in the Prosecution can in no way be surprised by anything that these witnesses would say. And the Prosecution has, after all, eight attorneys who are taking turns here, and there is no way they cannot go through the documents of witnesses who have testified before and prepare adequately. What possible prejudice could be done to the Prosecution? I would like to hear a specific example of shortage of time or any prejudice they would suffer. We are only asking Your Honours for the same standard to be applied as during the Prosecution case to Prosecution witnesses. Namely, that a statement would be provided as soon as the proofing is completed rather than asking us to give them a list of questions, retell, give an account of the interview, and put it in proofing notes. I don't think that is helpful to the Prosecution, and it is detrimental to the Prosecution, and after all, it's not necessary. Now specifically about this witness, Sajinovic. The witness spoke to the Prosecution two times exhaustively and not a single topic raised by Mr. Aleksic with the witness here in the courtroom goes beyond that. And we have been asked by the Prosecution to move the witness's testimony to Monday, if possible, so that the Prosecution would have the whole weekend to prepare. Now we are hearing their objection, why the administrative personnel had to work through the weekend. I suppose after all the OTP is also sometimes required to work the weekends just as we do. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After that long involved explanation, there's still no reason given why, given there's a two-week break, this witness -- their upcoming witnesses cannot be seen during the two weeks and properly proofed. Now, Your Honour, first of all, I don't know what Mr. Aleksic is talking about, about we asked for a witness to be moved to Monday. We made no such request. Second -- I believe -- I believe it was the Defence who said there was no point in having him called on Friday. Second, I would be grateful if Mr. Aleksic would stop shaking his head and interrupting. If he wants to say something, he can stand up and say it when I've finished. Second, Your Honour, the difference is - with one exception - one of the witnesses who's upcoming, the one that Mr. Krgovic wants to swap the order of potentially, I absolutely accept that he was interviewed and has testified before, but none of the others are in that position. The real difference is our proofing notes, with one exception, again, when the Defence asked for time, have been short additions to usually lengthy statements or transcripts. The Defence have therefore known in advance everything, effectively, that was going to be said by the witnesses. We do not. As I say, the one exception. And, finally, as far as this witness is concerned, as Mr. Olmsted said yesterday, and Your Honours heard a description from the witness of his meetings with the OTP, at least two of the topics were never ever, ever mentioned by the witness nor covered by him in any meetings that were held with the OTP. But I return to my original suggestion, Your Honours, which is that it be 72 hours in advance, given there's two weeks off. And by my reckoning, I think there's only about another five witnesses to go anyhow, and even some of them are doubtful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The concerns that the Prosecution has articulated are not unwarranted, but we agree with Mr. Krgovic that it would be arbitrary and probably result in unfairness if we were to impose a 72-hour rule as proposed by the Prosecution. And the -- what we would say is that as Mr. Krgovic has himself recognised, that, as soon as the -- they're in a position to provide a proofing note that they will. And the -- that they should do so. And that proofing note should be one of substance and not merely a skeletal outline which is, at the end of the day, wholly unhelpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say this. With these witnesses, regardless of your order, I will give my team orders to go through the witnesses, again through their evidence, and we will, of course, provide the Prosecution with the proofing notes as soon as possible. But the problem is that for any substantial proofing, is that the witnesses arrive here 72 hours in advance. 72 hours before testimony. And the real proofing takes place only here in The Hague and, of course, if we get any additional information during that session or during my stay in Banja Luka in my meeting with the investigators, we will provide the Prosecution with that information immediately. But I would not like to commit to a 72-hour notice, especially with witnesses who have not testified before in this case, and that's only two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought we already said we agreed with you, Mr. Krgovic, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to go behind Your Honour's ruling, but I want to point out this: It's not right to say the witnesses are here only 72 hours before. Sajinovic has been sitting here for a week at vast expense, no doubt, to the Tribunal and to certainly get himself some DSA. I'm afraid I don't -- just repeat that for this reason, Your Honours: There's two weeks where every single witness that's left for the Defence case could be seen, proofed, and shown the documents. Anyhow, but as I said, Your Honours have ruled and I'm not going to take the matter further. If Your Honours will then forgive me, that was the only reason I came into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, we should proceed with getting the witnesses. Before we do so, Mr. Krgovic, I'd like to make it clear that the Court actually shares the Prosecution's view on the quality and substance of the statements and the proofing notes. You have to be much more diligent in seeking the core substance of the witnesses' testimonies here in court because it's not only the Prosecution is confused, so is the Bench. So we need as well to have a much more elaborate basis upon which we can assess the witnesses' testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. However, unfortunately, the Trial Chamber has no access to the documents, such as statements of witnesses. Perhaps that is what is creating a problem. There is a proofing note relating to this witness that has 20 pages from the statement of his interview with the OTP and you didn't have a chance to get yourself acquainted with it, and I appreciate that. That means that means that the Trial Chamber did not have an opportunity to get into more details as regards the statement of this witness because it slipped my mind that you don't have access to the same documents that the OTP have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Which reminds me that I think that we made an agreement at the start of the trial that all witnesses statements, that is to say, not only Prosecution witnesses but also Defence witnesses, all these statements should also be addressed to the Court in advance of the witnesses' testimony so as to enable the Court to familiarise itself with the substance of the testimonies. So if you have such statements, I remind you that you should send them to the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Those were the statements given to the OTP in the course of their interviews. These are the ones that we are discussing, and these are the ones that we didn't use. In the future, we are going to explore who is it who is supposed to do that, whether it's us or them. But I'd like to underline, once again, that those were the statements given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that the statements were given to the Prosecution, but I would find it natural that it is the party calling the witness that has the duty to provide a copy of the statements to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, the -- would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sajinovic. Before Mr. Olmsted continues, I remind you of the solemn declaration you made yesterday. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if you see me wincing in pain as I try to stand up, at least now you know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, can you tell us when you first began working with Mr. Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was sometime in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You will agree that Mr. Radulovic, with the technical assistance of the other team members, produced a large quantity of intelligence reports in 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these intelligence reports were submitted under various formats, depending, in part, on their intended recipients.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's correct, to a certain extent -- to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And let's explore that. We've already heard you talk about the Milos reports. We'll just call them that. But they're the reports that have Milos either signed at the bottom or typewritten at the bottom, and those went to the Serbian MUP in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned Marko Lazovic. Was he one of the recipients of these reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, yesterday when I spoke about those reports, I told you who the recipient was, and the recipient was the state security centre in Belgrade. During our trips, I know that Mr. Radulovic would occasionally contact Mr. Radovic. I can only assume that Marko Lazovic was the person who received those reports, but I cannot tell you exactly to whom the operator sent those reports in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us which position Mr. Lazovic held in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but he was one of the executives in the State Security Department in Belgrade. However, which specific office he held, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But he was a high-ranking Serbian state security officer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you must admit that you cannot expect me to know what was the hierarchical structure of the RDB. I know that he was in an executive position. As far as which specific position he held, I cannot tell you anything more than I did, lest I should maybe make an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I accept that. Now, later, this Milos group also sent reports to the Serbian MUP under the name or symbol sigma; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to turn to a different type of report. Those reports that were Official Notes were directed up the RS MUP chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And some of those Official Notes would include the names of Mr. Radulovic, yourself, and the third member of the Milos group who was responsible for communications.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We saw that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And other Official Notes by Mr. Radulovic's team would include your assigned code numbers. So it wouldn't have your names but would have a number that indicated which officials were submitting the report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Official Notes, internal Official Notes, that circulated within the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Because, according to the rules of service, during a certain period -- although I don't know which specific period. You can find it in the notes. For that specific period the operatives, when making Official Notes, did not put their names but, rather, their code-names. And their supervisor, of course, was familiar with those code-names. It was basically a name but it kept changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm going to test your memory. Do you recall what your code-name or code number was back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I honestly can't remember. It's been a long time since. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Understandable. Perhaps I will show you some documents that will refresh your memory in a bit. Other Official Notes that were --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other Official Notes that were sent up the RS MUP chain of command just indicated they were from the state security. They didn't actually have the names or the code numbers of the officers who gathered the intelligence. In other words, they wouldn't mention Mr. Radulovic's or the other team members' names or codes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember that there were such Official Notes. If you would care to remind me, I would be only glad to comment on it, if they exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll do that just in a moment. Who decided which format to use for those Official Notes that were sent up the RS MUP chain of command? Was that Mr. Radulovic who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the chain of command within the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No I'm sorry, no. The when I say "the RS MUP," I mean the -- when I say the term "RS MUP" I mean the MUP of the Republika Srpska. So the one that was part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, with all due respect, I think that you said the Republic of Serbia. And I see that this is also recorded in the transcript and in the interpretation, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Not your fault. I apologise if I misspoke. At this time I'm just talking about the internal chain of command. If you could tell me: Was it Mr. Radulovic who decided what format to use for the Official Notes that he was sending up the internal chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I am sorry again, but I need an explanation from you. What do you mean by "format"? The use of a name or a code-name? Or are you asking whether we wrote our Official Notes or dispatches in a certain way? I don't know what you are referring specifically to. If you tell me that, then I can give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I meant the former. We've talked about now a couple or a few types of formats with regard to the Official Notes, whether they would include your names, whether they include a code number, or whether they include any reference to the team members at all. Would that be Mr. Radulovic's choice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue was decided by the leadership of the service, as I said earlier. For a period of time, the Official Note contained names and surnames, and then there was another period where code-names were used. So that was not within the purview of Mr. Radulovic but, rather, by the top executives of the service, and they were the ones who suggested which kind of format was going to be used, whether we would be using code-names or full names. If I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you did not type all of the intelligence reports that were produced by Mr. Radulovic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are still talking about the reports within the State Security Department, it is true that I typed only a few documents. There were members of the staff who were in charge of that. As far as those first reports are concerned, the one [as interpreted] that you called the Milos reports, I myself and another colleague of mine were providing this technical support to Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on those reports, those Milos reports that went to Serbia. Sometimes Radulovic typed up his own Milos reports; isn't that correct? Sometimes at least.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us be clear once again. You obviously mean that he typed them in the format that we had an opportunity to see here. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I mean that you had no involvement in preparing that report and producing it to the Serbian MUP. That Radulovic didn't use your services in that regard. He processed them himself.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know if I was clear yesterday, but let us put this matter in a context that both you can understand me and I can understand you. We are talking about the Milos reports sent to Serbia. The compiling of these reports and the gathering of intelligence for them was mainly done by Mr. Radulovic. My colleague and I typed those reports. I did it more often than he. And then my colleague would, through certain devices, dispatch them to Serbia. In other words, on very rare occasions, I don't remember actually not a single report that Radulovic himself processed, typed, and sent a report himself. That is the role of my colleague and mine as members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During Mr. Cvijetic's cross-examination, you mentioned that there was a period before the conflict broke out in the BiH that Mr. Radulovic was not sending internal reports up the BiH MUP chain of command. Can you tell us: During this period, was he still providing intelligence information to his superiors at the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand you completely. I don't remember saying to Mr. Cvijetic that before the outbreak of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Radulovic hadn't been sending regular reports within the service. I really don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, please correct me if I'm wrong. So prior to April 1992, Mr. Radulovic was still sending intelligence information up the MUP chain of command within the BiH. He was still sending intelligence information both to Serbia as well as to the BiH in Sarajevo, BiH MUP in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was sending reports to Serbia, as well as to his superiors at the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But was he also sending -- were his reports also going up the MUP chain of command to Sarajevo during this period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this yesterday when I gave my answers, and I said that I really didn't know whether those reports were being sent, as you say, to the MUP in Sarajevo. That was 01 of -- line of our work. Once a report is finalized and typed, it was sent to the head of 01 line, and he was the one who had discretionary right to whom he was going to distribute it, whether he was going to send it to the head of the sector, and then this head of the sector would, within his responsibilities, decide who would be the recipient. In other words, I really don't know where their final destination was and where they ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, you testified that -- yesterday that often the same intelligence information that was contained in the Milos group reports was also conveyed in reports sent to your superiors within the state security sector. Can you tell us, in 1992, for what kind of intelligence was this not the case? That you were not sending it up -- this same information up the RS MUP chain of command.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I am saying it once again. Those people who were gathering intelligence information, it is only natural that they obtain certain information in the process. Now, since we have two ways of reporting, it often happened that the intelligence contained in one report would be incorporated in another report. But I am afraid I'm really not in a position to tell you which ones were not sent to the first group of people and which one was not sent to another. Now what I can explain -- try to explain to you is that within the State Security Service, there were certain areas and lines of work that we discussed already, and there was the area covered by the National Security Service Centre. As for this group, we were not subject to any restricted area of the centre, nor were we tightly focussed on a specific area of investigation. Whatever information was available and we could get our hands on, we would send it to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So in gathering intelligence, you didn't limit yourself to what was in the jurisdiction of line 01. You would also report intelligence information that you had with regard to issues that maybe fell within other lines within the state security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which reports are you referring now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I was particularly referring to the Milos group reports going to Serbia. But, as you've already testified, you said that very often the same information was provided up the RS MUP chain of command. So, in that way, I suppose I'm addressing both. But I was focussing primarily on the Milos reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. As far as these reports are concerned, this is exactly what I said. The Milos group reports were sent to Belgrade from a wider area. They were not so narrow. As far as regular reports were concerned, intended for the service, it was done which the framework of the line of work. As authorised officials of the MUP, it was our right and obligation that in the event of our finding some security-related information, it was our duty to translate it into intelligence report even though it was beyond our line of work. So it was up to them later on to decide on the distribution and the availability of this intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what I'm get something at is that the purpose of this Milos group, as far as it's reporting to the Serbian MUP, was that it was there to share intelligence information with the Serbian MUP. It was not the intention of the Milos group to exclude the RS MUP leadership from that information. In other words, we are talking about a parallel reporting system. Information was going to the Serbian MUP and information was also going up the RS MUP chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about it a while ago. In principle, this kind of information was sent solely to the MUP of Serbia. So that was it. None of the executives within the State Security Service received this kind of information in this same format as the Milos reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let me be clear: I'm not talking about format here. I know there was a difference in format between the Milos group reports and Official Notes that were internally sent up the chain of command. All I'm talking about is the intelligence itself, the information that an event occurred or event is about to occur, that information was shared with both the Serbian MUP and probably, to a greater extent, to the RS MUP because that was the regular reporting chain. In other words, we have here a parallel reporting structure. Mr. Radulovic was both informing the Serbian MUP at the same time informing his superiors up the chain of command in the RS MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that, as far as I know, some of this information was sent in the form of Official Notes and dispatches through the line of work. However, whether all the information was subject to the same process, I am not sure. I cannot confirm that with any degree of certainty. I said that in my view, or, rather, I think I can say it's a fact, that we were present in the areas that were not covered by the Banja Luka Security Services Centre of which we were part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I believe you touched on this during your direct examination. But the reason why Mr. Radulovic was sending reports both to the Serbian MUP as well as reports internally to the RS MUP was because, at the time, it was perceived that Serbia and the Republika Srpska had a common interest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did touch upon the subject during examination-in-chief, that's true. We were aware that the federal state was still in place, and in our former state, it was quite normal that all reports from the republics go to Belgrade. Then there came a time when those communications, telephone communications, territorial communications, were interrupted, both with Belgrade and with Sarajevo, the base of the MUP, and that's, as Radulovic described to me, one of the main purposes of the group: To keep in touch with the federal service, with Belgrade, because we were still hoping that Yugoslavia, as Yugoslavia, will endure and that the war would be avoided. Now, whether Serbia and Republika Srpska had a common interest, I really would not like to voice any opinions because from my position I was not able to know the state interests of either entity. It would be pure conjecture, and I would not like to make any conjectures about the evidence I have given so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we would like you not to do so as well. But you mentioned that you were hoping -- still hoping that Yugoslavia, as Yugoslavia, will endure and that the war would be avoid. Well, Milos group primarily reported on events after April 1992, so when the conflict began. So at that stage the common interest was, of course, maintaining a Serbian -- a unified Serbian state between the Republika Srpska, Serbia, and the Serb portions of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, our interest was still in preserving the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, although in April 1992 the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina already started, and that opinion - as I told you - was shared by my colleague, Mr. Radulovic; namely, that the state of Yugoslavia was still able to endure. And I really don't want to go into any speculation about who else shared that interest. We spoke yesterday about the month of March of the same year. The Army of Republika Srpska had not been established yet and we didn't know whether it would be. And we, at least the people I knew, viewed the JNA as the saviour of our territories. An army that would save the people in those areas and help them stay there. And the JNA, indeed, acted that way. It kept its neutral position. And we knew that the JNA command was part of the federal state in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may have the help of the usher. I want to show you a couple of documents. And these are tab 46, which is P1381; and tab 47, which are 65 ter 1277. And let me just be corrected: On the tab 46, it should be 1381.1 because this one has protective measures. Sir, if you can look at the one that I wrote in pencil, the top "tab 46" first, and just take a quick -- a very quick read of it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you'll see at the end of it, it's signed "Milos."

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this reports, among other things, that the SJB Prijedor chief was involved in the murder of a large number of Muslim citizens in Koricanske Stijene. And if we can now look at 65 ter 1277, which has the same date as the -- the previous one. That's tab 47. Same date of 26 February 1993. This one is a SNB --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I believe that the accused don't see the document in Serbian in -- on the screen. Oh, it's here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you can look at tab 47, and this one -- in the heading it says it's an "SNB Banja Luka Official Note." Same date of 26 February, 1993. And, sir, you will agree that this is an identical report to the Milos report we just looked at, other than the fact that there's a newspaper article attached to it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. An identical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You will agree, then, that this is an example of the parallel reporting. The Milos report went to the Serbian MUP, while the SNB Official Note would have gone up the RS MUP chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I'm sorry I have to contradict you. But I've noticed some illogical things here, and some very odd things, if I may put it that way. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document you have shown me, tab 46, there's a date at the top. I can't see from the stamp which date, but I can only see that it's 1993 and it's called Official Note, and that's fine. However, at the end, as you said, there is a handwritten addition, Milos. And anybody who sees the document would think that it's one of the Milos group reports, as you said. However, I don't recognise this document as a Milos group report, and I belonged to the group, certainly, at the time, because I see a handwriting that is unfamiliar; Milos written in longhand, not typewritten as we normally did. We did sometimes write it in longhand, but it was the hand of the man we discussed yesterday. This handwriting, however, is unfamiliar. And I don't know that we -- that -- that we ever sent Official Notes in this format.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me address that issue first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this tab 47, 65 ter 1277 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object. Because the witness has not provided a single relevant piece of information about this document and even, to some extent, questioned the authenticity of the document. So we do not reach even the minimum threshold for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we already have P1381.1 into evidence. It contains the identical verbatim wording of this other report. We already have evidence that P1381.1 was a Milos report, and 65 ter 1277 is in the format that we've now heard would the type that would be sent up the internal chain of command. So this is an example of dual reporting, or parallel reporting, and the documents, in essence speak for themselves, and Your Honours can make that decision or evaluate them when it comes time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Isn't this, as -- sorry, Mr. Aleksic, you wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, I did not quite understand. Concerning this document that Mr. Olmsted is tendering, there's no signature, there's no name. The document tendered is in no way associated with this witness. There is no indication of his code-name or his name. For the witness to confirm that it's his report or a report by the group of operative officers to whom -- to which he belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's also outside the period of the indictment. These are documents from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honours will see upon reading the document, it deals with events in 1992, and you also have the testimony of the previous witness regarding this document. But, again, the Prosecution is seeking to admit it as an example of parallel reporting which is an issue that has been addressed by this witness, and this is an example of it to take into consideration. As far as the contents, of course the Prosecution is not concerned about that because we have P1381.1. What I'm concerned about is the fact that they are two different reports in two different formats that most likely went to two different recipients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just a question to clarify. Do I understand that tab 46, the one that is already in evidence, is the Milos report as sent to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And 47 is the one sent up the normal chain of command within the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And it is, unless I'm wrong, 46, the one sent to Belgrade, that the witness does not recognise, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I'm not really sure that I understand Mr. Zecevic's [sic] objection about 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have to intervene. The essence of the Defence objection is what the -- what Mr. Olmsted describes about this report is only his submission. It does not say in the report that it was ever sent anywhere up the chain of command. It's basically two copies of the same document. There is no indication here -- perhaps the Prosecution can clarify this, where does it say that it was sent to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia? What the Prosecutor is trying to put to the witness is only his submission. It's not confirmed by the document. And it says two copies. So it's possible that one copy is the one we have here, and the other is the one provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document under 46, I've already said, and the Judge on the right-hand side noted correctly that I don't recognise it as a Milos group, but the Prosecution and I did not discuss at all the document 47. I don't recognise that one either as a document written by me or my colleague, Mr. Radulovic. There is no name, no code-name, no indication to whom it was delivered, so I couldn't really claim that any of my colleagues drafted it. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it seems clear from the evidence that we now have that there's no basis on which this document could be admitted. Certainly not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, may it be marked for -- for identification so we can perhaps consider filing a bar table motion. Because, again, our point is the documents speak for themselves. We've heard evidence on formats and how they were -- different formats were sent up different chains of command, and these are identical reports with different headings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We hear you, Mr. Olmsted. And whereas I would be the first to admit that I'm still being educated as to the breadth of bar table motions, I would have thought that the same vice that infects the inability to tender it at this stage, if nothing new is coming, would not be cured by the time it comes for you to file a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with regards to a bar table motion, the issue is whether the Defence are prejudiced by it, whether it's relevant to these proceedings, and we go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, this document would not be admitted. First of all, the witness has testified about the parallel system of reporting. And the -- the proposition, unless we misunderstand, Mr. Olmsted, that it can be marked for identification pending the -- its reception through a bar table motion is, in our view, misconceived. And with that interruption, we are just at the break, so this may be a convenient time to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, if we might have a moment. The -- counsel would have been alerted to the fact that the break was extended and the reason for that will become obvious in a moment. Mr. Krgovic, you would recall that in July when we set out the plan for alternating this trial with the other trial in which Judge Delvoie and I sat, that we reminded counsel that they should be on the alert that the schedule would in all likelihood not run perfectly and there would be gaps which would have to be met. We have learned this morning that such a gap will occur next week and on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, that is, the I think 26th -- anyway, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday of next week, there will be no witness available in the other case to which Judge Delvoie and I are assigned. And therefore we are requiring you to make every effort to have a witness available to -- that we can hear in this trial on those three days. Today is Tuesday. That gives you a little more than a week to arrange it, and we would ask for a report, I suppose, on Thursday, that is, the day after tomorrow, as to -- as to the result of your efforts in being able to fill this gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best, and I will try to consult the Prosecutor in order to find the best possible solution in order to avoid any objections coming from Ms. Korner that they didn't have enough time for preparation for examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Seeing Mr. Aleksic's facial expression to which Ms. Korner objected in the previous session, I would think that it won't be very obvious to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm only a co-counsel here. I'm going to abide by what my learned friend Krgovic said. However, in view of the fact that I am leading the witness and the fact that I cannot be either in Serbia or Bosnia before the next Sunday, I really don't know how I can prepare the next witness in the course of two or three days. I appreciate what the Trial Chamber has said. I agree that Mr. Krgovic said that we will do our best. However, I objectively don't see how that would be feasible for me to prepare the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, you may resume your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 287 on the screen. It's tab 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 20 October 1993 memorandum from SDB Banja Luka Chief Kesic to the RS MUP deputy secretary of -- I guess at this time it was the SNB. And this is a proposal for promotion and decoration of Mr. Radulovic. And if we could just look at the second paragraph of this memorandum it reads: "In July 1991, he," referring to Mr. Radulovic, "was appointed before the Banja Luka SNB sector as a liaison officer for the contact with the MUP Serbia. In that function, apart from collecting ... intelligence and counter-intelligence information about the enemy's armed formations and intelligence service, he assisted in arming the Serb people in the broader region of the then BH and Slavonia. The cooperation with the MUP Serbia was professional and of mutual interest at the time." Sir, can you tell us, who appointed Mr. Radulovic to this liaison position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You will agree that the sharing of intelligence information between the state security in Banja Luka and the Serbian MUP would require a high level authorisation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I cannot fully agree with you. As far as I knew, and I knew from Mr. Radulovic that he had the authorisation of the chief of the sector of the National Security Service in Banja Luka, and if you think that this is the answer to your question, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In fact, we can see that from this -- this memorandum, can't we? We can seen that Mr. Kesic not only knew about Mr. Radulovic's reports to the Serbian MUP, but believed that such cooperation was important at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you just said can be seen from the letter which is currently on our screens. In other words, I didn't see, actually, who signed this letter. I can only surmise that it was Mr. Kesic because you said so. I can only see page 1. It is true that in the heading we have the National Security Service, but if I don't have a look at page 2, I cannot tell you who the author is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's just turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I have seen this document for the first time now, it is difficult for me to comment. But if you would allow me to read it, maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I just read the relevant paragraph that I want to ask you questions about, but I'm showing the second page just so that you can see that, in fact, at the bottom it was from Nedeljko Kesic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I can see that and I recognise his signature, and I can see that his name and his function has been typed in block letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Radulovic and, in fact, you as -- as his driver would on several occasions go to Belgrade to visit the Serbian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for Mr. Radulovic to do so, he had to get the authorisation of Mr. Kesic. Mr. Kesic had to authorise that trip.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my answer, yes. If we were away for a day or two from our workplaces, so to speak, we would typically travel in an official car. We had to have a proper written order, and it had to be authorised by the head of the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And given the nature of the intelligence information contained in Mr. Radulovic's reports to the Serbian MUP, Mr. Kesic had to be kept informed about what information was going via that route; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. I don't know myself that that is the case. I repeatedly said that I know nothing about it. I do know how the information was being forwarded and relayed to Belgrade, and that's all I can tell. And I'm talking about the information that pertains to this particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that copies of the Milos reports were sent to Mr. Kesic, just so that he would be informed about the contents of those reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'm hearing from you. My answer would be that, as far as I know, it's not correct. Yesterday, when I was examined by Mr. Aleksic, I explained in very clear terms how those reports were drafted, how their format was established, how they were typed, and then re-typed to the encryption device in order for them to be sent to the MUP of Serbia. After that, these reports ended up in the file and in the safe that was in Mr. Radulovic's office on the fourth floor. As far as I know, that was the end destination concerning the Milos reports. Now whether Radulovic gave them to Kesic as you indicated, I don't know. You would have to ask Mr. Radulovic about that. It's not my place to suggest to you, though, what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. And the third member of the team, the Milos team, the one responsible for communications since he was one who was filing the reports, he may also know whether, in fact, those reports were sent up to Kesic as well. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that either. You would have to ask him about this. If you are seeking my opinion, I think he knew even less than I did. But that's my opinion. Because his domain was to type the report into the device, to send it, and then to store it into the safe. So I wouldn't like, really, to speak on his behalf. You would have to take up this matter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now the safe in Mr. Radulovic's office, if Mr. Kesic wanted to have access to that safe, would you agree that Mr. Kesic, being your ultimate superior within the state security in Banja Luka, could access that safe?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree. As far as I know, he didn't have access to that safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mean so say that if Mr. Kesic came into Mr. Radulovic's office and said, "Please, may I see what's in that safe," Mr. Radulovic could refuse to show him what's in that safe? Based upon chain of command structure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this line of questioning is directed towards speculation. The witness is asked to answer what would happen if something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, this is not a joint witness. The person who should be objecting is Mr. Aleksic and not Mr. Cvijetic. Secondly, this is going to whether this individual, this witness, knows who could access something and the proposition is that someone who is above Mr. Radulovic, his superior, whether he could, if he wanted to, access that information in the safe, and I think Mr. Sajinovic has worked for state security long enough to provide an answer based upon what he knows about procedures, chain of command within the state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is, as Mr. Cvijetic has said, and I'm ignoring the point that you made about Mr. Cvijetic not being the person who can properly make an objection, but I would myself have thought the answer is self-evident, but if you wish to pursue it, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When you asked me whether Mr. Kesic had access, I told you that I couldn't agree with that assertion. And what I had in mind was that Mr. Kesic didn't have the key to the safe that was in Mr. Radulovic's office. Now, whether Radulovic was willing to show to Mr. Kesic the content of that safe had he been asked to do so, I really cannot tell. I know what would have happened in Mr. Kesic asked me to show him the contents of the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What would you have done?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not happen. I can only tell you hypothetically what I would have done, had that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you keep a short answer, can you just tell us whether you would grant him access. If you had access to the safe, would you give him access?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the hierarchical structure and the relations that were in place in the service at the time, regardless of the fact that Mr. Kesic was the head of the sector, I would deny him access to the safe without the consent and the presence of Mr. Radulovic. That would be my answer. The department in which I worked before 01 was 04, and Mr. Kesic was the head of that department as well, but he didn't have the key to the offices where we worked, and he could only gain access to those offices if the head of the sector gave him permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know how frequently Mr. Radulovic met with Kesic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I cannot tell you precisely. You're asking me how often they met. I even cannot confirm that they met at all. And, of course, I can't even tell you if they did how often that happened. Mr. Kesic was the chief of sector. We had senior staff meetings held at this level attended by sector heads. And if we're talking about 1992, Mr. Radulovic was not a section chief at the time, and he did not attend those senior staff meetings. He may have had some contacts of the sort on his trips, but I can't tell you how frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, I know you're trying to be very helpful by providing evidence today, but if you could please answer the questions as briefly as you can. If the answer is "I don't know," that's fine. I have to ask these questions because I wasn't able to meet with you and therefore I wasn't able to ask these questions to you before. So please don't read anything into it otherwise -- other than I'm just exploring some issues with you. While we still have this document in front of us, what do you know -- what do you know about Mr. Radulovic's role in arming the Serbian population in the BH as mentioned in the second paragraph of this report, or in memorandum?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. It was my best intention when you asked me to provide answers to you, but it's okay. As far as I'm concerned, I'm going to comply with what you said. I would accept your suggestion and had you told me earlier, I would have acted in the way accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And I was not -- it wasn't a criticism. It was just to move things along a little faster. Now, Mr. Kesic also utilized the Milos group to communicate with the Serbian MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that that's correct, no. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring up on the screen 65 ter 20293. That's tab 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, the document under tab number 50, I take it you are not tendering it because you're going to another document. I suppose you finished with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I move to have this tendered into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object to this document being admitted into evidence. First of all, they had Mr. Radulovic here as a witness, and this document should have been shown to him first. Secondly, the document is dated the 30th of October, 1993, and it says that in July of 1991, Mr. Radulovic had this contact. The witness said that he is not familiar with some of the aspects of this letter and the activities of Mr. Radulovic, and I don't think that there is sufficient nexus between this witness and this document in addition to what I already said. I would just like to reiterate that this document should have been shown to Mr. Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I just say that, Your Honours, again, as I've said I think two or three times already, these issues came up later in our case, after that witness that was referred, which probably shouldn't be referred to by name, testified in this Court, and we took actions to try to bring a witness - in fact, this particular witness - to deal with these issues at that time. And so now we're dealing with it at this time, and this is the witness to bring it in. He could authenticate it to a certain degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2395, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have in front of us 65 ter 20293. And as can you see, sir, a Milos report dated 5 August 1992 with the number 286/92. If we look at the first sentences, first couple of sentences, it says: "We have been asked by the chief of the Banja Luka SNB to urge through you that the agreed help in technical equipment be provided. In this regard, a request by the Banja Luka CSB was sent to you, approved also by the minister of the MUP of the SR, Serbian Republic of BiH." Sir, do you recall this Milos report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it as one of the Milos group reports, in terms of format. But as far as the contents are concerned, I'm not sure I've seen it before. And if the text could be shown a little larger, I would appreciate it. Thank you. I can see now. Yes, that's what it says, just as you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So this is an example of Mr. Kesic asking, presumably Mr. Radulovic, to send a request through the MUP -- Milos group to the Serbian MUP. Because obviously this was intended to be received by the Serbian MUP. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the MUP of Serbia should have received this. You are right about that. And in that sense, it's no different from other Milos group reports. But I couldn't say from the text that Mr. Kesic asked it from the MUP of Serbia. The way I read it, the chief of SNB Banja Luka, that is to say, Mr. Kesic, asked Mr. Radulovic to try to speed it up through the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think we're in agreement that that's what the intention was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not going to tender this one into evidence. I would like to bring up on the screen, however, 65 ter 20290. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, Mr. Radulovic also had the support of Mr. Zupljanin in sending information to the Serbian MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this document that's in front of you. It's a 4 July 1992 --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's a 4 July 1992 document. We see at the bottom there's handwriting. In Serbian it says, "broz 252/92." Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You don't have to read the document yet. All I'm asking you is you see handwriting at the bottom. Is that your -- the third member of the Milos group who was in charge of communication. Is that his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if you could take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see at the bottom it's typed: "Zupljanin." Will you agree that this information is being sent to the Serbian MUP at the behest of Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm seeing this report in this form with this signature for the first time. It wasn't shown to me by Mr. Aleksic during proofing, and even in that interview with the investigators in 2004, when I was shown a couple of documents, this one I did not see. This is the first time I see it on the screen, and it would be really hard for me to say anything about what it means. In fact, I'm surprised by this text and especially the signature. I really know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you'll agree that other than the signature, it is in the format of a Milos group report; and, in fact, it has the handwriting of your colleague from the Milos group on it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I will agree, because that is so. This is the format of our group's report. I recognise the handwriting, but until this moment, looking at the signature, I didn't know until now that something like this ever went out from our group. I -- I really can't imagine which one of us could have sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was not on the Prosecution 65 ter list. And as far as I was able to see, and as far as I know, it was not in the EDS either. And an additional argument, I'll repeat, Mr. Radulovic completed his testimony in May last year. The Prosecution completed their case in January this year. If they were not able to put this document on the list when Mr. Radulovic was here, they could have included it in a bar table motion at the end of their Prosecution case and -- to tender it. One more thing. We asked -- before the beginning of the Defence case, we asked the Prosecution to disclose to us every document referring to the names of any of our witnesses and Mr. Zupljanin. This document has not been disclosed to us and Mr. Zupljanin's name is on it. And on top of everything, the witness says he doesn't recognise it, and he sees this type of document for the first time and he doesn't recognise the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I explained before this witness began his evidence or at least before I started my cross-examination, these documents have been disclosed. They are available on EDS or we represented they were, and we provided a list with ERN numbers so they could look them up. And, in fact, the Defence came back to us and said a few of them weren't -- they weren't able to access and we provided those with them. So we know that they have this list, we know that they access them through EDS, and those that they couldn't they notified us about this. So this issue of disclosure with regard to these documents is not an issue. If Mr. Aleksic has a problem with this, during the break I will show him the list and I will show him where on the list this particular document is. With regard to fresh evidence, I've already raised - I think now this is the fourth time - the history of why we're presenting this evidence at this time. We did try to elicit this evidence during our case in-chief. We just weren't able to do so because we were unable to get the witness we wanted to do it. And this witness in particular, we sought to -- to call him in our case in-chief, in which case we would have met him, shown him these documents, seen if he could -- to what degree he can authenticate them, speak to them, and then we would have sought to add them to our 65 ter list at that time to address these very issues regarding access, access to these reports and to what the Milos group was doing. This witness was able to recognise the handwriting at the bottom. The format is the same. It just simply has Zupljanin's name down at the bottom, and the Trial Chamber will be able to look at this document and determine for itself what it represents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Olmsted, I don't understand your response when you say that the reason why it wasn't on your 65 ter list, and you give us one of the reasons, the fact that there wasn't a witness available to authenticate it, but this witness's testimony doesn't so authenticate it. So how does that advance your position in terms of the status of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe he sufficiently authenticates it. Yes, he said he didn't type it and he's never seen this particular document before, but recognises the handwriting at the bottom of it. He recognises the format to be that of the Milos group. Just because he wasn't directly involved in typing up or -- this particular document doesn't mean that it has enough authenticity be admitted for this Trial Chamber's consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may raise an objection of principle. And a specific one as well. We asked from the Prosecutor and we made a submission to this Trial Chamber that all documents concerning Mr. Zupljanin and concerning our witnesses be disclosed to us under Rule 66(B). This document fits that description. It explicitly mentions Mr. Zupljanin. Whether that's a mistake or not, that's another matter, but the Prosecution informed us that they have complied with this and that they have given us all the documents in that category. This document has not been disclosed so it can't be tendered and it can't be admitted. Second, the Prosecution had a witness, Mr. Radulovic, who testified here, and they could have shown him that document. You will remember at the end of Mr. Radulovic's testimony the Prosecution made a list of Milos group documents that they did not show him and that they still thought should be admitted through him. It was some nine documents that were admitted in that way. Also, they had a bar table motion through which they could have had it admitted. On top of everything, the Prosecution had given up on this witness and withdrew him from the list, especially because of the wrong-doing by Mr. Koehler. This witness used to be on the Prosecution witness list and during their interviews they showed him all sorts of documents. They struck him off the list, and he told them, "You can subpoena me. Just tell me, am I a witness or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to intervene here because that last statement by Mr. Krgovic he knows is incorrect as regards the procedure we went through with regard to calling this witness in our case in-chief. I'm not going to say more, but Your Honours are aware of the briefing on this matter, and -- we're not going to go any further on that. But I would ask that he does not make such statements that say why we did or did not call a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, just for my clarification, when we are talking about this witness now, you and Mr. Krgovic, are you -- are we referring to this witness or are we referring to the author of this document? Are we referring to this witness -- the witness actually on the stand or are we referring to the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're referring to this witness. The reason this document wasn't shown to the earlier witness was simply because this issue of reporting didn't even come up until late in his cross-examination. The Prosecution needed to review the evidence to how to respond to that and decided on a witness to call to rebut it. And that was what we filed I think in September or October of last year, a motion to call a witness to deal with these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I think the -- or one of the first rules about fresh evidence in cross-examination, certainly after the end of your case, would be that what you're trying to tender or -- or -- or prove there, should come -- should have a link with the -- with the -- the examination-in-chief. Should come out of the examination-in-chief; right? So my question is: Where is the link? Is this something that came up in the direct? Do I miss something there?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it did in the sense of who had access to these Milos reports, who was usually using this Milos group system of communication with the Serbian MUP, is all connected to the issue as -- Your Honours, may the witness take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- Mr. Sajinovic, could you please remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I should have made that request sooner because I think a lot of what we're talking about is probably not properly argued in the witness's presence. This issue goes to the issue of access, access to Milos group reports. Mr. Radulovic's access to Mr. Zupljanin. And this -- as we know, we have a number of these reports in evidence relating to events that are charged in the indictment, and so this is an issue with regard to this witness, what this witness came to testify about it. It's included in his 65 ter summary in the sense that he's going to talk about the Milos group and its relationship within the state security, and it came out in the questions asked by both Defences with regard to what was -- were Milos group reports sent, where were they -- who had access to them, who was within that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But within the -- your general approach to dealing -- in terms of your approach of that general issue which would have come up in -- been a part of the examination-in-chief, the question which the Bench has just put to you is in terms of this specific document. How does this document -- how do you link this document to the cross-examination? It isn't, to my mind, to talk about your general attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This document we purport shows that Mr. Zupljanin had access and contact with the Milos group and, in fact, utilized that group to convey information to the Serbian MUP. And this is an example of that. With regard to a matter that -- I tell you, to be honest, I'm not so concerned about the substance of it, just the fact that it was sent on behalf of the Mr. Zupljanin.
