Because certainly you can draw the conclusion that his name wouldn't appear at the bottom unless he somehow authorised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you had something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to all of this I would add, what does the contents of this document have to do with the evidence of this witness about the purpose and the sphere of interest of the Milos group? This says that some TV equipment should be taken out of some apartment. Even by that criterion alone, it could not fit -- it doesn't meet the requirements of being recognised as a Milos group report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We're -- well, on that last small point, Mr. Olmsted did say that he wasn't seeking to tender it for the contents. It was just in terms of showing method or system. But in any event, the Chamber is of the view that this document ought not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify a point of law, are Your Honours saying to us that we can only use or seek to tender fresh evidence that directly relates to the examination-in-chief or are we -- because I always assumed that we would be allowed to show evidence that's relevant that this witness may be able to provide evidence to or that might go to the witness's basis for knowledge or his credibility. So we can test the value of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect Mr. Olmsted I'm not going to be drawn into attempting to make an extemporaneous ruling on the question as you phrased it. This Chamber has given a considered ruling on the matter of fresh evidence, and I would suggest that that should be your starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this reporting system that was established by the Milos group, it was a two-way communication system, wasn't it? In other words, the Serbian MUP used the Milos group to pass on information to members of CSB Banja Luka, as well as RS MUP leadership; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with that. That's not true, as far as I know. And if you want me to explain, I will. Just say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, just hold off on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 20286; tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a report dated 3 April 1992. It has a document number 060/92. And it states: "Urgently pass on to Mico Stanisic to tell Karadzic not to accept at any cost Kovacevic for the position he is recommended. Convey this message to the Stanisic in the most discreet way." And the signature is typewritten: "Centre." Can you tell us who was Centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. The Centre was the state security sector centre in Belgrade. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were these kind of communications communicated through the same encryption device? In other words, it was over the telephone using the laptop device you described during your examination.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked me a moment ago about two-way communication, I don't know that there was communication from Belgrade towards the MUP, as you've said. What I know was going on, what happened, although very rarely, is that we, the Milos group, received a message from Belgrade. That message could have been a reply to something we had written or a suggestion. I have seen some of those, let's call them, reports from the centre, and that's correct. And when I say "centre," I mean the Belgrade centre, not the Banja Luka centre the State Security Centre or the Security Services Centre. But the document I'm looking at now is one I see for the first time. I did not see it at the time when the Milos group existed, and I did not see it during proofing here in The Hague. So I am seeing it for the first time. I'm not aware of the contents, and anything I could say would be my assumptions, if you want me to go into that. But, for now, that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you agree that the format is that of a report received from the Serbian MUP by the Milos group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. Because, as I said, it happened that the MUP of Serbia would send us a report very rarely, I repeat, and in that case, the signature would be Centre, that's true. But the one I see on the screen now, as I said, is one I'm seeing for the first time, both as a document, and I've never heard anything about what is said there. I never heard from Mr. Radulovic anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And -- and, again, you're relapsing into what I was asking you not to do, which is just keep the answers short and you answered it with: "Yes, I agree with that?" We see at the bottom it's handwritten --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I agree if I don't agree. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then that's fine. We see at the bottom it says -- it's handwritten 152/ -- I believe 73-4-128, and it says "copied." Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it says 52/79. I don't think it's 73, although it could be. But I really don't know the handwriting. It's not the handwriting of the colleague indicated at the top. It's not my handwriting. It's not Radulovic's. I have no idea whose it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what those numbers signify? Yes or no is fine.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which numbers? 152?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The numbers -- yes, that you just read out, yes. Do you know what they signify?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 20288. This is tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is another report that's signed or type written "Centre." And we see it's dated 3 July 1992. I'm not interested in the content of this report, but if you look under Roman numeral II the last sentence reads: "If necessary, engage Zupljanin." Will you agree that this is a communication between the Serbian MUP to the Milos group asking them to contact Mr. Zupljanin on the particular issue raised by this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see this under Roman numeral I, the thing that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Roman numeral II, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I've read it. Can you re-please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. My question is: Will you agree that this is a communication between the Serbian MUP and the Milos group in which the Serbian MUP is asking the Milos group to, if necessary, work with Mr. Zupljanin, their chief, on a particular issue, as mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I were to confirm that, that would be mere speculation. All I can confirm is that I recognise the handwriting, I can see the signature; whereas, I am not familiar with this document. What is being requested herein is also something that I have no knowledge about. I don't know that such things were being done, and what it says here "if necessary, engage Zupljanin," I really cannot believe that this refers to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. That would be all in the realm of surmise. There were a number of people named Zupljanin in the Banja Luka area. I'm not familiar with the gentleman mentioned in line 1. And also, as far as Zupljanin is concerned, had there been added the first name Stojan, I would have been sure. So I'm sorry to say, I'm not familiar with this document. And I think that it would be best if you asked Mr. Radulovic to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we're few minutes early, but perhaps this would be a good time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have P1371 on the -- hold on a second. Yes, P1371, tab 6, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, Mr. Radulovic also used his links with Belgrade to urge Mr. Kesic or Mr. Zupljanin to take certain actions. On occasions, when he was trying to accomplish a task, he would sometimes contact Belgrade and ask them to advocate his position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Would be so kind as to repeat the question because I'm not sure if I understood you correctly. So I am afraid in that case I might give you a wrong answer. So if it's not a problem for you, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be easier if I show you this document that's in front of you. It is a 15 April 1992 Milos report numbered 082/92. Can you take a quick look at this and tell us if this one you recall either typing or reviewing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the 14th of April; whereas, it says here the 15th of April. I don't know if we're talking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the transcript says 15th of April. I'll go with -- with that. Yes, the 15th of April. That's the one that's in front of you right now. Can confirm to us that you recall this particular report sent to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I had seen this document before. I recognise it as one being produced by the Milos group. But, as far as I can remember, and also judging by some grammatical, let's say errors, or, rather, judging by the style, it wasn't me who typed it. But I do recognise it as being a document made by the Milos group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It says in the second paragraph: "We ask you for an urgent contact with the Centre in purpose of clarifying and explaining the certain circumstances, which are neither in your, nor in our favour, if we want to succeed in executing the forthcoming tasks." Could you tell us the Centre that Mr. Radulovic is referring to here, would that be the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it couldn't be so. We discussed this many times, but let me be as brief as possible. He is not referring to the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you're saying that the centre he is referring to is the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So he is asking the Serbian MUP for an urgent contact with the Serbian MUP to clarify and explain a certain circumstance. Is that what you're saying that this is referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what Nenad Stevandic connection with the CSB Banja Luka security service. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that you had information that Colonel Stevilovic and Bogojevic were involved in the organisation of the SOS in Banja Luka. Were you also aware that Stevandic was also closely linked to the SOS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Stevandic is concerned, I know from that period, that Mr. Stevandic studied medicine at the faculty in Banja Luka. I know that he was the president of the athletic club in Banja Luka, but I don't know that he had any links with the SOS and the events unfolding in Banja Luka at the time. To tell you the truth, I did hear stories circulating around the town that he had links with them, but I myself had no direct knowledge about that. If he had any ties with them, I wasn't aware of the nature of those ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before you do that, could you clarify what you meant with your question, page 56, 14: "So he is asking the Serbian MUP for an urgent contact with the Serbian MUP to clarify," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, that's the way I interpreted the witness's answer, and he agreed that this was sent to the Serbian MUP asking for the Serbian MUP to clarify something with itself, I suppose, because he said Centre referred to the Serbian MUP. I guess it's open to whoever's interpretation they want to give it to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we should ask the witness whether that is what he understands because your question could been understood quite differently. I won't suggest anything, but please clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir I want to return to the question I asked you before. You said with regard to this document that when they ask for -- when Mr. Radulovic is asking for urgent contact with the centre, he is referring to the Serbian MUP as the centre. The Serbian MUP in Belgrade. And if that's the case, then the sentence as you interpret it should read: "We are asking you --" which would be, of course, the Serbian MUP, because this has been sent to the Serbian MUP, "We're asking you for an urgent contact with the Centre," meaning Serbian MUP. So basically they're -- he is urging them to contact themselves on this issue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't understand eventually what you said. When the -- they are to contact themselves. If I understand, it is Radulovic is seeking to establish contact with the Centre in Belgrade. That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But your prior testimony was the Centre was, in fact, who was receiving the Milos reports. In other words, the Centre was the Serbian MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So wouldn't you agree that in this context, the Centre means something other than the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree because I already told you that the Centre maintained communication with the Milos group, and the only centre that was doing that was the State Security Department in Belgrade. It says here: "We kindly ask for an urgent contact with the Centre," and so on, and from this I understand that Radulovic is asking for him to go personally to Belgrade and meet with someone there. And this is the only conclusion that I can draw from what is written here. The mention of any other centre would make no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if that clarifies matters for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm satisfied, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let's have 65 ter 20294 on the screen. This is tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 5 August 1992 Milos report number 283/92. And if you can just look at the final sentence, it reads: "Could you please urgently intervene in that regard with the chief of the CSB, as well as with regard to resolving the problem of housing for myself and Miso?" Would you agree that this is an example where Mr. Radulovic is contacting Belgrade asking them to, in turn, contact Mr. Zupljanin on a particular matter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this one of the Milos reports; that's true. Now one can see from the contents that Radulovic is asking the State Security Department in Belgrade to intervene with the CSB chief. That's what it reads. However, I didn't have an opportunity to see this note or this report before, and I'm slightly surprised at its contents. As you read it, it seems that there was a request for solving the housing problems for two colleagues of ours, and speaking of 1992, when all this was happening, I myself also didn't have my housing problem resolved. Therefore, I find it really hard to comment this, given that I am seeing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 10101, tab 14. And perhaps we can take a quick look at the second page of the B -- oh there is only one page. If we can scroll down so we can see the bottom of this B/C/S version. Oh, page 2. Yes. Great. Sir, this is a 19 May 1992 Milos report, numbered 140/92. And if we can return to the first page. In the second paragraph, this report proposes arming the able-bodied inhabitants of - I'm going to mispronounce it - of Vrbanjci and surrounding villages. If further states that: "We also propose that you use a special unit to render inactive and neutralise the Green Berets in Vrbanjci." And if look at the very bottom, so the second page of the B/C/S, it states at the bottom: "The proposals concerning a special unit and weapons refer to the Banja Luka security services centre." Mr. Sajinovic, can you tell us -- Mr. Sajinovic, can you tell us, is Mr. Radulovic referring to the CSB Banja Luka Special Police Detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only suppose that he does refer to it. Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look now at P76, which is tab 17.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we stay a little bit longer with this document? On page 1, you haven't read the whole document, and I notice something which strikes me as interesting, and I would like to comment, if that is all right with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well the Defence will have the opportunity to re-examine of you. For the purposes of my questioning, I think we can proceed. Unless there's an objection with my line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the witness has -- whereas I'm always very reluctant when a witness is volunteering evidence, since it is something that he is -- apparently wants to speak to in terms of making us understand this document, It would be useful to deal with his. Let's hear what he has to say now. Could we have the -- okay, it's back on the screen. Okay. Yes, Mr. Sajinovic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. When Mr. Prosecutor was reading the second paragraph, where it says: "Please help the inhabitants of Vrbanjci as much as you can, especially by arming them ..." But I see one sentence here added by Radulovic which says that: "We propose that arming of the able-bodied inhabitants of Vrbanjci and the surrounding villages be carried out within the framework of regular mobilisation." As far as I can understand this document I would like to underline, especially having seen it before, that Radulovic is requesting here for regular mobilization to be carried out of citizens and, at that time, in charge of mobilization was the Secretariat for National Defence, i.e., the army. I'm afraid if we leave out this second sentence, it might appear that Radulovic was asking for some paramilitary formation to be set up in that area. I'm grateful to you for giving me this opportunity to clarify this section of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P76 on the screen. Tab 17. This is a 9 June 1992 Milos report. And the first sentence reads: "Following our proposals and the proposals of others, the SDS is due to start an operation soon with the aim of taking over power in the Kotor Varos area ..." And if you read further down, it states: "This operation should be carried out in a synchronised manner with the help of the Banja Luka CSB." Sir, would you agree that the Milos group's proposal to use CSB Banja Luka Special Police Detachment made its way not only through the Serbian MUP but back to the CSB Banja Luka because here he is reporting that the proposal was being followed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor, but not for a moment can I conclude based on anything that is read here that an intervention of the CSB Banja Luka Special Police Detachment was requested. I might be wrong, and I would be grateful if you would point me out in the direction where it says that a certain request was complied with. As far as I can remember, this was in the month of June, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, well, I was referring to the previous document that you looked at. We read the sentence that says: "We'd also propose that you use a special unit to render inactive and neutralise the Green Berets in Vrbanjci." And further it states that this proposal, concerning the use of the special police unit, refers to the Banja Luka CSB. I'm just asking you now whether this document we have in front of us shows that that proposal in fact was received?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I would put it, and I cannot establish a link between these two documents. If you're asking me to comment anything with relation to the previous document, I'd like to see it again. As it is, I cannot establish any chronological order with regard to the previous document. I'm really sorry I have to say that. I can't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's quickly look then back at 65 ter 10101. And what I was focussing on was the second paragraph where states further down we also propose that you use a special unit to render inactive and neutralise the Green Berets in Vrbanjci? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see that part of the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when we turn to the second page of the B/C/S, and you see the note at the very last sentence that says: "The proposals concerning the special unit refer to the CSB Banja Luka." And this is dated the 19th of May. The second document we looked at was dated the 9th of June, so subsequent to this one. And I'm trying to see whether in the second document when you referred to our proposals, which were being followed, whether that is what's referred to in this document here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second document was written 20 days later after the other one. If the security situation was, indeed, as it was described in this document, 20 days seems long to me for a reaction. Things were unfolding very fast. So it can hardly be the case. And as for your other remark, it is a Milos document. The date, the signature, everything fits. And it was sent to the MUP of Serbia, and this remark about me, the special units and weaponry, you can see it says CSB Banja Luka. It can assume [as interpreted] that it was a special unit from the CSB Banja Luka, but it was an explanation to the recipients of this note. I already explained that mobilization was normally carried by the army, and I suppose this suggestion was an alternative. If the mobilization fails for some reason, he was suggesting that a special unit of the police be used and that would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's return to P76. If you look at the first sentence, I will repeat. It says: "Following our proposals and the proposals of others, the SDS due to start an operation soon with the aim of taking over power in the Kotor Varos area ..." Can you tell us what were your proposals?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the sentence goes on: "... as well as defusing the interethnic tensions in SJB and other agencies." Now, after all this time and in few of the position that I occupied, I could hardly comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you don't recall what your proposals were? Or at least Mr. Radulovic's proposals.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't remember what Mr. Radulovic suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness could speak to the first document, 65 ter 10101, so we would seek to tender that into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Since we last canvassed this issue earlier today, Mr. Olmsted, we've had the benefit of having to hand the views which the Chamber distilled in Rule 15(A), of guide-line 15(A). Could you tell us how your application falls within that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This -- I'm reminded this was on your 65 ter list, so you needn't trouble yourself there. Could I hear what the response is from the other side, in terms of your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will agree, of course, that the document is on their list, but I can only repeat my previous objections: Why did they not use it with Mr. Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't want to go into this full discussion again, but we've expressed our reasons why we didn't do it at that time and how we had to proceed from that point forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2396, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P1384. That's tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a Milos report dated 13 July 1992, numbered 272/92. We see at the very top of it it states: "Please forward this information to the chief of Banja Luka CSB ... Stojan Zupljanin." You'll agree that this request is requested to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So Mr. Radulovic is asking the Serbian MUP to provide this piece of correspondence to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It then states: "In view of your absence from the Centre's area, I'm obliged to address you in this way ..." He's obviously there referring to Mr. Zupljanin. Mr. Zupljanin's absence from the Centre's area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you will agree with me, at least on this occasion, the Centre they are referring to is the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I won't agree. I don't understand why you keep trying to put in my mouth words that I have never said. Everything written by Milos was addressed to the Centre in Belgrade. Not a single Milos report was ever sent to the CSB centre in Banja Luka. I repeated that several times. I'm aware that I'm under oath. I'm aware that I'm supposed to speak the truth and I'm telling the truth. And I don't understand why you keep insisting on something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not trying to do that. I'm just trying to make sense of what it says. It says: "In view of your absence," and I assume he's referring to Mr. Zupljanin, and you confirm that, "from our centre's area..." And when referring "to our Centre's area," I assume that that meant CSB Banja Luka. Are you telling me that's not the case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what I'm trying to say. In that, you are right, Mr. Prosecutor. But as you've read this communication is sent to the MUP of Serbia, the state security sector, Radulovic. I know this text from before. I know about the contents and the form. Radulovic is asking the MUP of Serbia to pass this information on to Mr. Zupljanin and then goes the text. Considering that you are away from the territory of our Centre, and they mean the centre in Banja Luka. Mr. Zupljanin is temporarily absent from that territory. And I'm sorry if I misunderstood you a moment ago if that was what you meant. But, otherwise, centre in all the conversations in the Milos group denoted the Centre of state security in the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now in this report Mr. Radulovic is asking Mr. Zupljanin to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, are we to assume that then Mr. Zupljanin was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, your understanding is correct. At the time when this report was written, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was in Belgrade. It is dated 13 July, and, as far as I know, and I did have occasion also during proofing with Mr. Aleksic to see some other reports, during those days in Belgrade there was a meeting. I can't say exactly at which level, but it was attended by the senior staff of the MUP of Republika Srpska, including Mr. Zupljanin. So he was away at that time from the territory of our centre. He was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to look briefly at the contents of this report. Mr. Radulovic is asking Mr. Zupljanin to allow him to replenish the reserve police in Teslic with 80 soldiers. And it states that: "Their engagement would be good for preventative reasons since individuals from this company or the entire company have gotten out of control and become a paramilitary formation." Can you tell us, if you recall, how this group had gotten out of control?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly I couldn't comment. I know which group Radulovic means. I know who the commander of that unit was, and it was a military unit. So it was in the purview of the military commander in the area of Teslic. They were part of the military. And as you say here, their engagement -- it says for preventive reasons, so I can't conclude from this that they had become renegades already and turned into a paramilitary formation. It is said that there are some indications that that unit could go absent without official leave from the regular military unit and turn into a paramilitary one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But your answer is you don't -- don't recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes. I'm saying I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. We have your other answer so ... We'll go from there. I want to show you 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Olmsted, please. Mr. Witness, when commenting this document, this document is about the reserve police and speaks about one company of 80 well-trained and well-equipped soldiers. Just one moment. I'm sorry, I misread. Back to you Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 10187, tab 19 on the screen, please. And I'm particularly interested in the second report. It looks like there's two reports on the same page. It's dated 3 July 1992. It's from again Centre. And it is report number 250/92. I'm sorry, I probably read the wrong number. Just a second. Let me check my notes. Sorry, it's report number 249 /92.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the seconds report states: "We confirm that Bozovic and his group are being active in a coordinated fashion, linked up with the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and ourselves." So this is the Serbian MUP providing the Milos group with this information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm with us that the Bozovic that is referred to here is Radojica Bozovic, the leader of the Red Berets that you testified about during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I see the last name here. I don't see the first name. I can only suppose that's the man. And perhaps it's important to tell you this. I see both of these reports for the first time. During proofing, or earlier, I don't remember -- I'm sorry, I first read the first report, and now I'm reading the second. I really couldn't say that I saw either of them earlier. I'm not aware of the contents. The first report speaks about a convoy of 120 vehicles in July and that sounds a bit odd to me. And to your question, the answer could be that I'm not sure whether it's Mr. Bozovic, but it's true we discussed yesterday that Radojica Bozovic did go to Doboj with a group and that they carried out training of soldiers who had no military experience and were supposed to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you testified yesterday, you stated that from what you've recalled they -- they, meaning the Red Berets and Bozovic, acted independently at the time. Now having looked at this Centre report, does that refresh your recollection that, in fact, Bozovic's group was linked to the Serbian MUP and here the RS MUP as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Prosecutor, to be quite honest, I testified yesterday, and I've said what I know and what I remember. This report not only does not refresh my memory. It confuses me completely. And to be quite, quite honest, during our time in Doboj, I saw Mr. Radojica Bozovic a couple of times and his group, but from nothing, not from the uniforms they were wearing or their conduct, could I conclude that they had anything to do with the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it would be to be expected that if they were associated with the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they would seek contact with us or perhaps assistance from us or vice versa, but I'm not aware of any such thing. Radulovic maybe knows different, but he was here. I'm sorry, I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that you saw Mr. Bozovic a couple of times in Doboj. Can you tell us where you saw him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, I encountered him and his group once in town, on the outskirts; another time I saw him close to the front line, where fighting was going on to open up a corridor; and from the local residents and some acquaintances and some contacts of ours, we received information that they were training soldiers who, as I said, had no military experience and were about to go to the front line. Nobody ever told me -- look, to be -- I mean, quite sincere I'm sorry I'm taking up your time. But especially at that time, it was normal that anybody who had anything to do with the MUP and had an official ID would use it and sometimes even abuse it, but I never ever heard that any of them were identified as members of the MUP. And I'm seeing this report for the first time, and the one -- the one before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this relates to his testimony in examination-in-chief, I would seek to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object to the admission of this document. I agree that Mr. Bozovic was discussed during the examination-in-chief. But as for this specific document that is being tendered, the witness did not confirm anything from it, and I believe that the required nexus between the witness and the document does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness may take off his headphones, I'll respond. Your Honours, that is precisely the point. The witness said during examination-in-chief that this group was acting independently. This document, which is not in dispute that it is from the Serbian MUP, refutes that, so it goes to credibility on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2397, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I apologise for keep making you to do that, but we sometime have to resolve issues that are best reserved for the Trial Chamber alone. I want to return briefly to the organisation of the state security in Banja Luka in 1992. We've already talked about section 01 which was headed by Vojin Bera. His ethnicity was Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the jurisdiction of section 01 was aimed at the collection of intelligence on the enemy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence and counter-intelligence, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And there was also a section, 02 which was enemy emigration, and that was headed by Slobodan Sakan, who was a Serb; is that correct? And we're talking about after April 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Slobodan Sakan not Sakan, but that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. There's also a section 03 and that was internal enemies, which included activities of the various ethnic groups, their nationalist or extremist activities. And that was headed by Dusko Milinkovic, who was also a Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sure if Dusko Milinkovic was still there, or was it Emir Zahirovic because Emir Zahirovic was head of that section 03 for many years. He was a Muslim and he's still a Muslim. He lives in Banja Luka still. And Dusko Milinkovic succeeded him, that's true, but I don't know when, and I seem to remember that after that Mr. Emir Zahirovic was assistant head of sector of the state security sector in Banja Luka or chief of operations or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Milanovic replaced Mr. Zahirovic. Do you recall, was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dusko Milinkovic, not Milinkovic and not Milanovic, it's Milinkovic. So Dusko Milinkovic did come to that post after Mr. Zahirovic, but I really can't be sure anymore. Look, it was such a long time ago. If I'd only continued to work in that section, perhaps I could be more precise, but, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And section 04, that was the technical department that you first worked for and after April 1992 that was headed by Mladenko Milanovic who was a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of section where I worked was Milan Baric, a Croat, from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm referring to the -- after April 1992. So I know that by that time you had moved to 01 section. So after April 1992, was Milanovic in that position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenko Milanovic was acting chief after Milan Baric left for a while, but he was an operative technical employee, and he was more of a technical staff member. But I really can't say whether it was before April or after April. All I know is that once I left, Milan Baric was head of section 04.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there also in 1992 an analysis department at state security Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, there was -- not a section. There was one analytical job. One person was an analyst. Independently of these sections, there was analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who did they report to? Who did that person report to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that person was directly responsible to the head of sector. The state security on national security sector, we use both terms because they alternated at various times. He was directly responsible to the head of the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us which of these sections was responsible for gathering intelligence on crimes committed against non-Serb population, against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sure. I'm really not sure. I don't know if that line of work within the section or department or whatever had already been established. I am not sure, so I really wouldn't like to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that Mr. Radulovic and the rest of his team would report internally any crimes they learned about in which non-Serbs were victims. You didn't withhold that information. You had a duty and would carry out that duty to provide that information to your superiors.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, if we gathered information not about crimes but about any security-related matters, as we did with all the other information, we would translate that into Official Notes or report along 01 line of work. However, if Radulovic decided or concluded that it was necessary, this information would be sent to Belgrade, as we discussed before. I would like to note here that I cannot claim with any degree of certainty that Radulovic invariably sent every -- information through the line of work, that he sent it to Belgrade. But I think that there was some overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In particular, Mr. Radulovic was troubled in 1992 about the crimes being committed by the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment against non-Serbs. Wasn't he concerned about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this topic was not broached during the examination-in-chief, and I don't know to which particular part of the examination-in-chief it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Need I respond to that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whereas, the -- as I understand the Rules of the Tribunal, the ordinary rules about cross-examination being at large is modified, in that it should closely reflect the examination-in-chief, I -- I -- I don't understand that rule to require every specific question in cross-examination to -- to have a -- a reference point in the examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll ask my question again. Do you recall in this 1992 time-period that Mr. Radulovic was particularly troubled by crimes being committed by the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that, and I really couldn't comment on that. I know that Mr. Radulovic, as well as the other members of the group, as well as the executive staff in general of the Banja Luka CSB, had certain problems and concerns in the aftermath of the operation in Teslic which involved the bringing in and criminal processing of Serb criminals who committed crimes against non-Serbs in Teslic. That much I know. Now, as for the crimes committed, as you've said, by the special unit from Banja Luka, believe me, I don't know anything about it. Nobody had any problems in that area, given that I am not aware of those crimes, I am equally not aware of any consequences that resulted from them. And I also believe that I said something similar to your colleagues in the interviews that we referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, in fact, that's what I'm looking at right now. And isn't it, in fact, the case that in 2004 you told Inspector Sabir that when you went around collecting intelligence information that you often heard about the crimes being committed by this special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. As I told you, the words that I uttered were typed on a laptop by your colleague. I was never given an opportunity to read what he wrote, to learn what the contents were, and to verify. I remember him asking me about the crimes, whether I had heard of them. I said that I didn't. He kept insisting on asking me whether I knew anything about the police activity, and I told him that at that time one could hear all sorts of things about the activity of the police from people being involved as criminals to those who were acting as true heros. And when asked where I told that, I told him I heard those stories in the street, in bars, in discussions with my father, or on TV. Believe me, I said that at the time - and I can repeat it here - that, in my view, the majority of members of the special unit were honourable people who joined it with respectable intentions. I did say that some local criminals infiltrated these kind of units. I allowed for that possibility, but my general opinion is the one that I have just expressed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you described for us the formal reporting line for Mr. Radulovic and his team, up the RS MUP chain of command. But isn't it the case that in 1992, in practice, Mr. Radulovic could and did convey intelligence information directly to Mr. Kesic and Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we discussed this formal exchange of information yesterday and the hierarchy that existed at the time. I personally don't know if Mr. Kesic had any direct contacts or whether he directly passed on information. We discussed about the information provided by Mr. Kesic to Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bulic, and I allow for a possibility that that took place in the course of some informal context, but I am not aware of Mr. Radulovic - how shall I put it? - having some lateral contacts with the chiefs of the state security or the CSB chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you deny that you made that statement, that Radulovic conveyed intelligence information directly to Mr. Kesic and Mr. Zupljanin. You deny you made that statement during your 2010 interview?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who conducted the interview? Which interview are you specifically having in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interview with the OTP, with the investigator from the OTP. In August 2010.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I deny it because I didn't say that for sure. I couldn't have said it. Yesterday, Mr. Prosecutor, I explained that in the telephone conversation with Ms. Jasmina she read out to me the Prosecutor's report which contained lots of untruths, the majority of what is contained there was not consistent with what I said. It might have been an issue with the translation or whatever. Now what you are trying to impute to me is really inappropriate. This also refers to the report made in 1994. It wasn't recorded. I remember Mr. Koehler just taking some brief notes. I read this report and signed it [as interpreted], and we can talk about it in a relevant fashion, but as for the other things, I don't think it's really appropriate to discuss something that I am quite sure didn't happen in that way. After all, your colleague told me that he didn't want to take a statement off me, that I was not supposed to give a statement, that it wasn't being recorded on the tape, that that was an informal conversation, and that he wanted me just to clarify certain points that you, as the Prosecution, had with regard to the testimony of my colleague Predrag Radulovic. I agreed to that conversation, which I now regret because, obviously, it was misinterpreted and was lied to or deceived by your colleague on many occasions. I don't want to mention his name. And I am really reluctant to go on commenting on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, as a Prosecutor, I need to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague Olmsted. On page 77, line 18 in the transcript, in the second sentence there is something that the witness didn't say and it reads: "I read and signed the report," and the witness didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just clarify that. I think there is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You did not sign a report or a statement in your 2010 interview with the OTP inspector -- investigator?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, and Your Honours, several times so far, I said that in 2010, I didn't give any statements. Therefore, it was not possible for me to sign anything, nor was anything that the investigator wrote on paper was shown to me. They told me that it wasn't being recorded at all, that this was not a proper statement but just an attempt to clarify certain things with my assistance of what my colleague said in his testimony. You can ask me the same question as many times as you wish, and my answer will always be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, the last question that counsel asked was to correct what was patent error in the transcript. He wasn't badgering you. Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the proceeding questions are also not intended to badger you either, if that can be translated somehow into B/C/S. I'm simply asking you questions to confirm whether you did say something or not, because this is how I find out because, as you know, I haven't spoken to you about these issues. Can you tell us whether you told the OTP investigator in 2010 that there was an unofficial direct line from Radulovic, to Kesic, or Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can only repeat my answer. I don't remember saying something of that nature to the investigators. And I'm sure that that was the case. It was quite recently. Had it been a conversation that took place eight or ten years ago, it is possible for me to err. But this was recent, and I clearly remember that conversation. So I can confirm that I really didn't say that. If I had been asked that, I would have answered that I didn't know anything about that and that I was not part of those informal contacts. And I'm telling you today again, that I don't know whether Radulovic had this sort of contacts and with whom at the level of the centre where we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 20287, tab 9. This is a 30 April 1992 Milos report, number 103/92. Can you confirm that this is one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the format of our report, and I can confirm that this is one of the reports produced by our team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This report is transmitting the text of a statement to the Bosanska Krajina public that was written by -- it says written by our group. I presume that's the Milos group. And it says: "At the request of the CSB Banja Luka chief." Do you recall Mr. Radulovic, or perhaps yourself, drafting the text of that statement for Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really don't remember that this kind of announcement or text was written. No, I can't recall. No. Definitely not. Now, judging by the date, and there's reference to the order of the Ministry of the Interior, It means that this happened after the declaration of war by the minister of the interior, National Defence of the Republic of Serbia. I remember that towards the end of April, some dispatches were received which we construed to be the declaration of war, and this date indicates, to me, that this might have to do with that. But I really don't know what kind of announcement or text would have been written. If it was written at all, I, for sure, was not one of its authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move to 65 ter 20296, tab 35. This is a 30 September 1992 SNB Banja Luka Official Note, numbered, I believe, if I read it correctly 428/92. And it was submitted by operatives 28, 33, and 38. And I believe the handwritten number on it, that is the handwriting of the third member of the -- Mr. Radulovic's team.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you may recall way back at the beginning of today, of -- we talked about the various formats that Official Notes appeared in that were sent up the internal chain of command in RS MUP. And we talked about one format was where your names would be omitted but numbers would be used instead. Having looked at these numbers, 28, 33, 38, does that refresh your recollection that those were the numbers for the three members of the Milos team back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, when we discussed this topic, I said, and I can repeat once again, I really don't remember which numbers we used. However, I can assume that these are, indeed, the numbers that we used. As you said, this is the handwriting of the third member of our team. And I have no reason to disbelieve that these are genuine numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at the second page. We can see at the bottom who the -- to whom this report was sent to. The first, it was sent to the CSB chief; second, it was sent to the chief of state security; and, thirdly, it was sent to -- or a copy for the operatives. Who made the decision on your team as to who should receive their reports? Because here we can see this one is being sent to the CSB chief.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. One can see, as you said, who the addressees were, and it was decided by Mr. Radulovic, as we already mentioned, because he was the team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in this case, Mr. Bera is not on this distribution list.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as much as I would try to give you the shortest possible answers, I really need to explain this for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and yourself. When we discuss this distribution system, it says here that one copy was sent to the chief of the CSB, one copy to the chief of the SNB, and one copy to the operatives. However, each and every single report of this nature was given to the head of the department. In this particular instance, as you said, to Mr. Bera. The word "sent to" means that the authors of the document propose for it to be distributed to the persons listed below. And that was based on both our suggestions and Mr. Radulovic's suggestion as well for it to be sent to the chief of the CSB and one to the chief of the SNB. The first filter, so to speak, would be the chief of the department, in this case, Mr. Bera. Then it would go on to Mr. Kesic, the chief of the SNB, who would decide whether this kind of report should be forwarded to the chief of the CSB and so on and so forth. Alongside Mr. Kesic, there was this person in charge of analysis who would process such reports and provide this aggregate information either to the CSB chief or to someone else designated by the chief of the CSB. You are right. This is what it says here. But I, as an operative, cannot confirm to you at this point whether these reports actually were received by the addressees listed there. Our position was that it should have been done, but our hands were tied. We couldn't have it done it without the chief's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well that brings us to a convenient point, and we take the break and return in an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, continuing our discussions this morning about where we go after today, when we rise this afternoon, at the end of today's sitting, we would take the adjournment to 2.30 tomorrow afternoon. And we will sit from 2.30 to 4.00, and then 4.30 to 6.00. And then at 6.00 we would take the adjournment to 1.45 on Thursday. Sorry, thanks. 2.15, the usual starting time on Thursday. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 20296 back on the screen. And if we can turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before the break, we were looking at this document as an example of an instance where Mr. Radulovic put on his distribution list both the CSB chief, as well as the state security chief. And I want to just confirm your testimony in that regard. If I understood you correctly, the reason Mr. Radulovic did not include Vojin Bera on this distribution list was because the report was going to Mr. Bera regardless. It was going to go to him no matter what.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The report of the operatives within the RDB department.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you explain to us, it says at the bottom, it says: "One copy to operatives." Who's that? Who is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are referring to operatives mentioned in the heading of this document as the authors of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 765 on the screen. This is tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 17 November -- I'm sorry, 17 October 1992 official record with the handwritten log number, I believe it says 458/92. And we can see at the top, along with Mr. Radulovic's name, is your name. Can you confirm this is a report by your group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can see in the -- we can see in the last paragraph that you're reporting that a fairly large Croatian military unit has surrendered and that you had information that Muslim armed forces in Kotor Varos, in particular Vecici, want to surrender on the condition that they be allowed to proceed without hindrance towards Travnik. Do you recall participating in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom, it has another distribution list. And the first one on it is 01. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means the 01 line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, not the entire line. That would mean that this is to go to Mr. Vojin Bera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the chief of the 01 line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see below it, one copy was to be sent to the analysis department. We talked about that earlier. That was the analyst who reported to Mr. Kesic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And on this particular one, we don't see that Mr. Kesic is included in the distribution list. Or Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, as I have said earlier, and this applies in this case as well, at the end of each document, at the end of each official record, it was customary to put the distribution list and to put the -- among the proposed addressees, the author of the document. Was it really necessary for this to be delivered to us who wrote the document? It was natural for it to be sent to the chief of the department, and then it was his decision whether he would send it to the analysis department or not. And then one copy would be either sent to us or not, if there was any need for us to be further engaged in that task. We knew that automatically this official record would be sent back to us, but it could have been also sent to somebody else, if our chief of the department thought it was necessary to send it to somebody else as well. I think I explained something similar a bit ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I think I understand you. You're stating just because it doesn't have CSB chief or state security chief written on here, doesn't mean that they did not get. It is possible that they still got it, depending on whether 01, Mr. Bera, decided to forward it further on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Just like in the previous case. Even though they were listed, that did not necessarily mean that they received it. In this particular case, as you have correctly stated, if Mr. Bera thought that it needed to happen, then that's how it was. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour. If my learned friend refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I was referring to 65 ter 765.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I see the record doesn't reflect Judge Hall's response. And I think that's why there is a silence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I said admitted and marked. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2398, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'd -- I think it's appropriate to admit as well the last document I showed the witness which was 65 ter 20296.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are objecting to this document being admitted, the main reason being that it's not on the 65 ter list. It's 29 -- 20296. The number is quite high. And the second matter is that Mr. Olmsted is not interested in the content of this document. This pertains to Western Slavonia, events in Western Slavonia in late September of 1992. Therefore, the main grounds for objection is that it's not on their list and the Prosecution need to explain why, in this stage of proceedings, they want this document. They had Radulovic here and why haven't they done this until now? That's the main objection we have and the second objection concerning the contents of this document is an additional one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, has the Prosecution asked for admission of document 65 ter number 20296 in -- into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood it. We had nothing against the document which was listed as 765 on the 65 ter list. That was the previous document. Yes, the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, obviously I was confused about which document we were looking at, but what is the -- what is your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the witness may take off his headphones, I'll explain. The reason I'm tendering this document, as Mr. Aleksic points out, is not for its content. I'm not concerned about its content. I'm concerned about the distribution list. This witness's testimony is that this was just a wish list of persons that he hoped would -- they would hope would get the documents. And the reason they did not include Mr. Bera on that is because he would get it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but do we need the document for that? We have the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you have a point there, Your Honour, but because the testimony is derived from an actual document, to have the two documents side by side might assist the Trial Chamber. But if Your Honours feel that that has come out sufficiently through the oral testimony, I will defer on that issue, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Indeed. This trial is replete with documents and if that were the only criteria -- yes. So the order for admission is vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 10199. That's tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a 3 November 1992 Official Note with the handwritten number 474/92. Can you -- oh, I'm sorry. Yes, could you please put your headphones back on. I apologise for leaving you stranded there. What we have in front you right now is a 3 November 1992 report by Mr. Radulovic and the other members of his team. Can you confirm this is one of your reports that went up the RS MUP chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This note raises a concern about civilians, mainly old people, women, and children, from Vecici. Do you see that? It's in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us with regard to those civilians, mainly old people, women, and children, what were their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this report, or, rather, this Official Note, I really couldn't comment on it because I was not familiar with this. I think that I saw this Official Note during proofing, but that was the first time I've ever seen it, and I wasn't aware of this event and what is stated here. As far as I can remember, the source listed here in the first paragraph of this Official Note was a person who had direct contact with Radulovic. Therefore, I couldn't really tell you anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down on the English a little bit. We see in this distribution list it first goes to the chief of the CSB, and, secondly, it goes to 01, Vojin Bera, and then it goes to the analytical department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There was this operative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And at the bottom it goes to the operative group which would be Mr. Radulovic. He kept a copy for himself.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he received it, then, yes, he kept it. We commented the previous two documents, and my answer would be the same. I can repeat it. This is the proposal of the author to have this delivered to the people listed in the distribution list. Now as to who actually received it, I really couldn't say anything about that. I cannot confirm that all of the people listed there, indeed, received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the beginning of today, back in the transcript page 17, line 9, you told us with regard to state security documents, documents that go up the RS MUP chain of command, you typed only a few of them. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you didn't type them, who was typing these Official Notes that would go up the state security chain of command; if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that during today's hearing, namely, that, as far as the Milos group report, everything was done within our three-member group. As for these reports, for these Official Notes -- and they were typed up in the same place where all other Official Notes were typed up. That is to say, in the state security in Banja Luka, where the notes of all authorised officials were typed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who would type up -- so there was a typists pool, administrative pool, that would type up all the reports that were submitted to them by the various SDB inspectors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. It was -- I don't understand what a typists pool is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. That's an English word that's probably hard to translate. But essentially SDB inspectors would draft their reports, and they would submit it to an administrative unit within the state security who would actually type up the reports for the inspectors. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in principle. Reports were written up. We did not have any computers. We didn't have even have many typewriters. We did have the typists bureau. They were occasionally typed up but mostly they were handwritten, and on occasion people dictated to somebody their notes and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then, if I understand the process, the person who typed up the report would then deliver it. Or would it go back to the inspector for proofreading or something like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was a bad question. After it was typed up, would it return to the SDB inspector for him to make sure it was typed properly; or would the person who typed it up simply distribute it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was supposed to come back to the author of the report so that he would read it and check for any mistakes. And then I guess that person would then forward it to the head of the department. Section head.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So in these cases that would be Mr. Radulovic, since he was primarily the author of these notes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In most cases, he was the author. And he was the one who would read and then forward it to the head of section, as I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P1353-12. This is tab 32. And I'd like to turn to page 2. This is a 24 September 1992 Official Note. And we see at the bottom it has Mr. Radulovic's name and then your name and the other member of your team. Can you identify for us the handwriting at the bottom left side of the page? And in English, it is written "we cannot do this." And there's a signature and a date.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you this is the handwriting of Mr. Milan Krnjajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could scroll to the top of the page, we see it's written on the right side upper corner: "Kesic, deliver a copy of Official Note to security organs." And then there are some initials. Do you recognise the initial underneath that note?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kesic, the copy of the Official Note to be sent to the security organ. As far as I remember, as far as I remember the handwriting, I think that this is the handwriting of Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to 65 ter 20020, tab 34. This is a 28 September 1992 Official Note. Can you confirm whether this is one of your team's reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. Not until I see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is it not on your screen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see on the screen is the first page of a document, but I don't see the last part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There's only one page, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that this the entire document, what I see on my screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the entire document as we have in our possession, yes. If there's a second page, we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but based on this, I cannot say with any certainty that this is a document drawn up by us, by me and my colleagues, because in the heading it only says that this is the sector where I worked. And the date seems right, but there's no signature, there's no name, there's no code. So it looks incomplete to me. It's very hard to identify it, no matter how hard I try.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You see in the first line it says: "Through our collaborator, 'Div' ..." Do you recall that Div was one of Mr. Radulovic's sources back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think that there was a person with this pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it was a standard practice back in this time-period for SDB inspectors not to share their sources. In other words, they would not give one of their sources to another inspector to use, but they would keep them secure for themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's how it was done during that time, before, and after that time, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now this note reports that Predrag Kujundzic, a worker of CSB Doboj and members of his group are involved in looting. In particular, it mentions -- this was down during a cleansing operation in - and I'm going to mispronounce it, I know - Civcije. Can you tell us, was Civcije a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say because, as it happens, a relative of mine comes from that village, and she's an ethnic Serb. Now whether there were Muslims living there, I don't know. It's possible, but I don't believe that was it a Muslim village because, as I have told you, as I've explained a relative of mine is from that village. She currently lives in Banja Luka and is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You will agree that Mr. Radulovic was concerned about crimes committed by Kujundzic against non-Serbs in Doboj during this time-period. You recall that that was an issue for him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would readily agree with you, but, as I have already said, I cannot claim with any certainty that this is a note produced by Mr. Radulovic. I don't see any names or any other distinctive marks based on which I could conclude that. I keep reading and re-reading it, trying to identify the author, but I cannot confirm that he was the author of this document, nor can I confirm that this gentleman whom you have mentioned, that he was a member of police. The gentleman mentioned in this note. Yesterday we spoke in private session about some groups from Doboj, and even yesterday, I never mentioned that I knew that he had been a member of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, your body language, while Mr. Olmsted is asking questions and even when the witness is giving answers, is extraordinary and remarkable, and remarkable means that it can also be seen by the witness, and I don't think that's appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I will agree with you. However, I was concerned because these names were discussed in private session. I didn't want to interrupt my learned friend, but what I wanted to bring to your attention is that all of these matters were mentioned in private session. I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't react on the first time I see it, Mr. Aleksic. It's in your personality, but just make sure that it is within certain limits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Sajinovic, we've already established, however, that this source, Div, was one of Mr. Radulovic's sources.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SAJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said so. Yes. I said that I knew that the source under this pseudonym was, indeed, used by Mr. Radulovic. I cannot claim with certainty that there did not exist another source with the same pseudonym or that some other of my colleagues also used the same source. I said a bit earlier, and as Mr. Aleksic emphasised now, if you intend to keep asking me questions about these persons and these names, then we should go into private session because I do not want to mention the names that yesterday were already discussed in private session. I wouldn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
